# Compounding Pressures and Scaling Limits {#sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales}

::: {.epigraph}
> "[F]eedback is a method of controlling a system by reinserting into it the results of its past performance. If these results are merely used as numerical data for the criticism of the system and its regulation, we have the simple feedback of the control engineers."
>
> — Norbert Wiener, *The Human Use of Human Beings*, revised edition [@Wiener1989HumanUse, p. 61]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Why has system and chip design become harder to carry through, and where might AI assistance be useful?*

**Core thesis:** *Compounding pressures across physical scaling, specialization, software co-evolution, and verification demand new abstractions, but assistance helps only when it targets the work that actually limits the next design decision.*
:::

System and chip design increasingly depends on choices that must be evaluated together. Device scaling still improves transistor density, but no longer supplies the same broadly reusable gains in frequency and energy efficiency. Specialization, local data reuse, and new packaging can recover performance, while binding the result more tightly to software and physical implementation. Each promising architectural change can therefore require work in several disciplines before its value is known.

Establishing the system value of these changes requires executable software, representative workloads, and physical and functional checks. Comparing candidates draws on finite simulation, verification, and review capacity, so the cost of learning whether a change helps can become the limiting pressure. The resulting bottleneck differs across projects (@fig-ch02-cover-map). Point AI assistance, an AI-native design system (both defined in @sec-moonshot), or conventional automation can improve the study when it addresses that bottleneck and its gains justify the total cost. Complexity alone does not establish a need for AI.

![**Compounding pressures shift the architectural bottleneck.** Fading automatic technology gains, coupled design obligations across hardware and software, and finite simulation and verification capacity converge to limit design velocity. AI assistance helps most when it targets the specific engineering work delaying the next supported decision.](images/ch02-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch02-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which fading technology gains, coupled design obligations, and finite checking capacity converge on the work limiting the next supported decision."}

Instead, the right tool depends on where the study actually stalls, because a team waiting for a compiler path faces a different problem from one waiting for simulations or expert review. The pressures traced in this chapter explain why such delays arise, but only measurements from the project can show which work must improve.

## Where Engineering Time Goes in Modern Chip Design

The cost of architectural exploration is visible in a familiar design choice. When an architect considers expanding an on-chip level-2 (L2) cache to relieve memory bandwidth pressure, a capacity-focused simulation may favor the larger cache because it reduces misses. In silicon, however, the additional static random-access memory (SRAM) bitcells consume die area, lengthen interconnects,[^fn-rc-delay-c02] and increase leakage current. Within the thermal envelope of a passively cooled mobile device, that extra leakage reduces the power budget left for the compute cores. A simulated drop in cache misses therefore answers only part of the architectural question.

[^fn-rc-delay-c02]: **Interconnect resistance and capacitance**: A wire has electrical resistance, while neighboring conductors contribute capacitance. Charging that capacitance through the resistance takes time. Narrower wires increase resistance, and long connections add both resistance and capacitance, so a larger storage structure can take longer to access even when its transistors switch quickly.

Software offers another way to attack the same memory bottleneck. Loop tiling can reduce the working set that must remain on chip at one time, allowing a smaller cache or buffer to retain useful data, although the tiled loops can add control overhead. If the schedule uses direct memory access (DMA) to feed an explicitly managed local buffer or scratchpad, it also incurs transfer-descriptor and coordination costs. To weigh a larger L2 cache against a tiled software schedule, the architect needs both an executable schedule and characterized physical memory macros. Beyond building those inputs, the architect has to decide which hardware–software pairs are worth testing and which measurements will separate them.

Weighing hardware against software in this way cuts across the boundaries that earlier abstractions were built to separate. Each jump in abstraction kept implementation complexity manageable by hiding lower-level detail behind automated tools. Register-transfer level (RTL) descriptions let engineers specify synchronous circuit behavior without placing individual gates by hand.[^fn-rtl-c02] Logic synthesis and place-and-route tools then generated the gate-level layout. As @sec-moonshot showed, those abstractions succeeded because trustworthy verification tools, such as equivalence checkers and timing analyzers, checked the lower-level implementation automatically. Today's cross-layer, specialized architectures strain that model because hardware and software choices interact across the boundary, forcing many more coupled candidates through slow implementation tools and the timing and power signoff checks that precede fabrication.

[^fn-rtl-c02]: **RTL as an architectural contract**: RTL specifies synchronous state updates and transfers between registers. Changing pipeline stages or interface timing can require restructuring these transfers, so an architectural alternative may need more implementation work than changing a parameter.

Testing each of those coupled candidates follows a *design path*, a sequence of work that proposes an architectural change, builds candidate artifacts, runs the relevant tools, and compares the results, such as evaluating two L2 capacities under a representative workload in the cache study. That path becomes a closed *design loop* only when the returned evidence updates the represented design state and triggers the next step, as when high leakage leads the architect to record the smaller cache and evaluate a tiled software schedule instead. Whereas a fixed parameter sweep collects measurements across a preset grid, a closed design loop uses each result to determine subsequent work.

Every turn of that loop spends engineering time, electronic design automation (EDA) tool licenses, and human review on inputs that span RTL source, execution traces, timing constraints, and specifications of which blocks may power down. The breakdown of classical transistor and wire scaling explains why more architectural choices now require such cross-layer experiments.

## The End of Free Scaling and the Push Toward Specialization {#sec-fracturing-technology-dividend}

For roughly thirty years, processor performance advanced under classical Dennard scaling, in which each process generation delivered smaller, faster transistors at constant power density (@tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison) [@Moore1965Cramming; @DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. Today, device technology still supplies transistor density, but it no longer delivers proportional gains in frequency, single-thread performance, or energy efficiency. To extract more performance, architects now have to make choices that tightly bind microarchitecture, software mapping, and physical implementation together.

### The Collapse of Dennard Scaling and the Shift to Specialization

Classical Dennard scaling balanced denser transistors against lower power per transistor. Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ reduced area by $1/\kappa^2$, while lower capacitance and supply voltage reduced switching energy enough to permit a higher clock frequency at constant dynamic power density [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling]. The dynamic-power relation $P_{\mathrm{dyn}} = \alpha C V_{dd}^{2} f$ makes voltage's role explicit: its contribution is squared, alongside switching activity $\alpha$, capacitance $C$, and frequency $f$.

The classical balance broke down in the mid-2000s because supply voltage could no longer fall alongside feature size. Lower voltage slows transistor switching unless the threshold voltage also drops, but lowering that threshold increases off-state leakage.[^fn-subthreshold-leakage-c02] Device physics thus forces a trade-off among switching speed, active power, and leakage. Once voltage reductions stalled, process shrinks alone could no longer deliver simultaneous gains in clock frequency and energy efficiency [@EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon; @HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge].

[^fn-subthreshold-leakage-c02]: **Subthreshold leakage**: Below its threshold voltage, a transistor's current falls exponentially with gate voltage, at best by a factor of ten for every 60\ mV at room temperature, and that behavior does not scale with device dimensions [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling]. Lowering the threshold by 60\ mV can therefore raise off-state leakage by up to about ten times. We read this limit on the threshold as one reason supply voltage stopped falling with each process generation.

The comparison in @tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison isolates what changes when voltage and frequency stop scaling. Its simplified post-Dennard case holds activity, voltage, and frequency fixed while retaining idealized area and gate-capacitance scaling. Leakage and interconnect capacitance are excluded from that calculation, although a real implementation must account for both.

| Device Parameter | Classical Dennard Scaling ($\kappa > 1$) | Simplified Post-Dennard Case | Limiting Physical Constraint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transistor Area ($W \times L$)** | $1/\kappa^2$ | $1/\kappa^2$ | Gate pitch scaling continues |
| **Supply Voltage ($V_{dd}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Leakage and switching-speed trade-off |
| **Gate Capacitance ($C_{\text{gate}}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1/\kappa$ *(idealized)* | Gate and interconnect capacitance scale differently |
| **Operating Frequency ($f$)** | $\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Thermal dissipation and leakage limit frequency gains |
| **Dynamic Power Density ($P_{\mathrm{dyn}} / A$)** | $1$ *(constant)* | $\kappa$ *(under stated assumptions)* | Dark silicon and thermal limits |
: **Classical Dennard scaling versus a simplified post-Dennard case.** Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ historically kept dynamic power density constant while increasing operating frequency. With voltage, frequency, and activity held fixed in the displayed post-Dennard case, dynamic power density rises by $\kappa$; leakage, interconnect, and nonideal geometric scaling make real product behavior implementation-dependent. {#tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison tbl-colwidths="[24,24,28,24]"}

Under the table's post-Dennard assumptions, power per transistor falls more slowly than transistor density rises. More transistors can therefore fit in the same area without all being able to switch at once within the same power budget. Leakage and interconnect costs further affect the usable fraction in a physical chip.

@fig-microprocessor-trends maps this architectural evolution across three eras. It joins fifty years of microprocessor scaling data from Karl Rupp's sample (1971–2021) [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData], less that sample's GPU and Xeon Phi records, with a 2012–2026 frontier compiled from the published specifications of `{python} mt_acc` accelerators, including GPUs, of which `{python} mt_trans` supply transistor counts and `{python} mt_power` supply power ratings [@NVIDIA2016P100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2017V100Whitepaper; @JouppiEtAl2021TenLessons; @JouppiEtAl2023TPUv4; @NVIDIA2020A100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper; @AMD2025CDNA3; @NVIDIA2024B100; @NVIDIA2012KeplerGK110; @NVIDIA2013K20XBoardSpec; @AMD2021CDNA2; @Myrhang2023AMDInstinctHPC; @Intel2023Gaudi2Datasheet; @Intel2024Gaudi3Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet; @NVIDIA2025BlackwellUltraBlog; @NVIDIA2026RubinBlog; @Cerebras2019WSE; @Cerebras2021WSE2; @Cerebras2024WSE3; @AbtsEtAl2020GroqTSP]. The power ratings of the AMD MI100 and Habana Gaudi 1 come from vendor documents named in the dataset and are not cited here; neither sets a point on the plotted frontier. In the *device-scaling era* (1971–2005), single-thread performance, clock frequency, and transistor counts all climbed by orders of magnitude, though at different rates. Around the 2005 Dennard boundary, clock frequency stalled near $3\text{--}5\ \text{GHz}$ in this sample. Single-thread performance growth fell from about 52% per year (1986–2003) to about 23% per year (2003–2011), and to single digits by the late 2010s [@HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. This slowdown ushered in the *parallelism era* (2005–2016), as architects turned to multicore integration and sampled hardware thread counts climbed to 96 by 2016 and 128 by 2020. Those counts depend on the exclusion, because the Xeon Phi records left out of the plot reach 272 threads in 2016. We date the *specialization era* from about 2016, as dedicated datapaths became an increasingly important use of growing transistor budgets. That date is our framing rather than a measured inflection, since no plotted series breaks there. The exclusion does not make the CPU series pure. Its last transistor point, 57 billion in 2021, matches a laptop system on chip whose count includes a GPU [@Apple2021M1ProMax], so part of the CPU series' approach to the accelerator frontier near 2021 reflects what the sample counts as a CPU.

Accelerator counts reach 336 billion transistors (4 trillion for wafer-scale parts), and power ratings reach $1{,}400\ \text{W}$. The text cites six dated design reports and all but two accelerators; the hatched band after 2026 marks the emerging AI-native design frontier rather than a fourth measured trend.](images/fig-microprocessor-trends){#fig-microprocessor-trends width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Log-scale chart with CPU sample maxima ending in 2021 and accelerator specification frontiers extending to 2026. A hatched band after 2026 marks a hypothesized AI-native design era; a separate rail dates six AI-assisted design reports."}

The divergence of these curves after 2005 [@Sutter2005FreeLunch] is consistent with the *dark silicon* limit that @EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon model.[^fn-dark-silicon-c02] Once supply voltage stopped scaling, thermal budgets capped the fraction of a chip's transistors that could switch simultaneously at full clock frequency [@HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. Duplicating general-purpose cores during the parallelism era converted extra transistors into thread-level concurrency, but serial code sections and shared-memory traffic soon limited the return on adding more homogeneous cores.

Specialization answers that limit by spending the transistor and power budget on dedicated datapaths. Packaged accelerator transistor counts climb from 15.3 billion in the NVIDIA Tesla P100 (2016) to 208 billion in the dual-die Blackwell B200 (2024) and 336 billion in NVIDIA's Rubin GPU (2026) [@NVIDIA2016P100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024B100; @NVIDIA2026RubinBlog]. Cerebras goes further, integrating 4 trillion transistors on a single wafer-scale die [@Cerebras2024WSE3]. Over the same span, published accelerator power ratings rise from the P100's $300\ \text{W}$ thermal design power (TDP) to as much as $1{,}400\ \text{W}$ total graphics power in the Blackwell Ultra generation (2025) [@NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @NVIDIA2025BlackwellUltraBlog]. Although those ratings describe nominal hardware envelopes rather than measured application efficiency, they reflect an industry directing its silicon budget into regular matrix and tensor arrays that amortize instruction fetch and decode across hundreds of arithmetic units, trading clock-rate scaling for dense spatial parallelism and local data reuse.

The hatched band in @fig-microprocessor-trends identifies the design process as a possible next source of improvement, rather than a measured successor to specialization. The dated reports alongside it describe early applications to placement, design support, circuits, and generated processors or accelerators [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @Verkor2026DesignConductor; @Verkor2026DesignConductor2; @DeepMind2026AlphaEvolveImpact; @OpenAI2026JalapenoFirstResults]. Most come from the teams that built the tools. The two generated designs from Verkor stop before silicon, one at a layout with reported timing and the other at a mapping onto a field-programmable gate array with an area estimate, whereas Google and OpenAI report AI assistance on chips that reached silicon, and the placement result remains disputed (@tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors). None of these reports establishes that an AI-native design system reduces total project cost against a comparably equipped conventional team. The pressure that motivates such a comparison begins with the physical and coordination costs of exploiting larger transistor budgets.

[^fn-dark-silicon-c02]: **Dark silicon**: Silicon that cannot all operate concurrently at full performance within the available power and thermal budget. Power gating, clock gating, and reduced operating rates are among the ways a design manages that limit.

### Diminishing Returns Inside General-Purpose Cores

General-purpose processors continue to improve through branch prediction, speculative execution, wider issue, and better memory hierarchies. These mechanisms can expose and exploit more instruction-level parallelism, but each one adds hardware that tracks and orders the extra work in flight.

The out-of-order issue window illustrates that cost. More entries let a core look farther ahead for independent instructions, while wider issue allows more instructions to execute per cycle. Completing instructions must broadcast result tags to waiting entries, however, and selection logic must choose which ready instructions proceed. Enlarging the window increases the load on those broadcast wires; widening issue adds comparison, arbitration, and bypass paths. Circuit analysis shows how wakeup, selection, and bypass delays limit the return on wider issue [@PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective], while wire delay restricts how far a signal can travel in a clock cycle [@AgarwalEtAl2000ClockRateVersusIPC].

Replicating cores does not escape this cost; it moves it into coherence, synchronization, and workload partitioning. General-purpose architectures continue to advance, but each gain in parallelism, whether inside one core or across many, has to pay for the structures that coordinate it.

### The Shift to Domain-Specific Accelerators

When a workload performs regular, predictable calculations, a specialized datapath can strip away most of that per-instruction coordination hardware and devote the silicon to dense arithmetic arrays. The trade works only if the memory system can keep those units fed.

The trade has produced a diverse population of accelerators rather than one canonical template, a shift the Project Brainwave team characterized as rapid architectural diversification [@ChungEtAl2018Brainwave]. Publicly announced AI chips, cards, and systems spread across the power–performance plane from milliwatt edge devices to multi-kilowatt data-center platforms (@fig-accelerator-landscape) [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS].

```{python}
#| label: fig-accelerator-landscape
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **AI accelerators span more than six orders of magnitude in peak power.** Each point represents a
#|   publicly announced accelerator entry from the MIT Lincoln Laboratory survey, plotted as peak performance against
#|   peak power on log-log axes; the 180 entries across 170 accelerators span about $1\ \text{mW}$ to $23\ \text{kW}$ and
#|   $6\ \text{GOps/s}$ to $3.5 \times 10^7\ \text{GOps/s}$ [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS]. Marker shape and color denote form factor (circle chip, square card, triangle system), filled versus hollow markers
#|   distinguish training from inference parts, and dashed diagonals trace constant energy-efficiency contours
#|   from $100\ \text{GOps/W}\text{ to }100\ \text{TOPS/W}$.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-log scatter plot of about 180 AI accelerators, peak performance in giga-operations per second versus peak power in watts. Points span from subwatt embedded chips at the lower left to multi-kilowatt data-center systems at the upper right, more than seven orders of magnitude in power and nearly seven in performance, with the lowest power resting on a single entry. Dashed diagonal lines mark constant energy efficiency from 100 giga-ops per watt to 100 tera-ops per watt. Chips are circles, cards squares, and systems triangles; training parts are filled and inference parts hollow."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
from _python.labels import place_labels

apply_style()

# Data: MIT Lincoln Laboratory AI accelerator survey, 2025 edition
# [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS], one row per publicly announced accelerator with a
# stated peak performance and power. Values are dataset-transcribed.
# Accessed 2026-07-19. Source data: book/contents/chapters/02-pressures/data/fig-accelerator-landscape/chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
rows = []
with open(_root / "book/contents/chapters/02-pressures/data/fig-accelerator-landscape/chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for d in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        try:
            perf = float(d["peak_performance_ops_per_s"]) / 1e9
            power = float(d["power_w"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        rows.append({"label": d["label"], "perf": perf, "power": power,
                     "form": d["form_factor"], "iort": d["inference_or_training"]})

forms = {"Chip": COLORS["workload"], "Card": COLORS["methods"], "System": COLORS["evidence"]}
markers = {"Chip": "o", "Card": "s", "System": "^"}  # shape as well as hue
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0))
xline = np.array([1e-3, 1e5])
for eff, lab in [(1e2, "100 GOPS/W"), (1e3, "1 TOPS/W"), (1e4, "10 TOPS/W"), (1e5, "100 TOPS/W")]:
    ax.plot(xline, eff * xline, ls=(0, (5, 4)), color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    x_pos = max(2.4e-3, 10.0 / eff)
    ax.text(x_pos, eff * x_pos * 1.3, lab, fontsize=4.6, color=COLORS["muted"],
            rotation=34, rotation_mode="anchor", va="bottom", ha="left", zorder=1)
for form, color in forms.items():
    for iort, filled in [("training", True), ("inference", False)]:
        pts = [d for d in rows if d["form"] == form and d["iort"] == iort]
        if not pts:
            continue
        xs = [d["power"] for d in pts]
        ys = [d["perf"] for d in pts]
        if filled:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolors="white", edgecolors=color, linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.95, zorder=3)
for txt, x, y in [("Very low power", 0.02, 3.0e3), ("Embedded / autonomous", 3.0, 1.2e1),
                  ("Data-center cards", 5e1, 2.5e6), ("Data-center systems", 1.5e4, 2.5e5)]:
    ax.text(x, y, txt, fontsize=5.2, fontstyle="italic", color=COLORS["muted"], ha="center", va="center", zorder=2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(8e-4, 7e4)
ax.set_ylim(3, 1e8)
ax.set_xlabel("Peak power (W)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Peak performance (GOps/sec)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.2, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
handles = [Line2D([0], [0], marker=markers[f], ls="", markerfacecolor=c, markeredgecolor=c, markersize=5, label=f) for f, c in forms.items()]
handles += [Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=COLORS["ink"], markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Training"),
            Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Inference")]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3, borderaxespad=0.4)
curated = ["Maxim", "GAP9", "Jetson1", "Perceive", "A100", "TPU4", "H100",
           "AMD-MI300X", "B200", "Gaudi3", "CS-2", "DGX-H100", "GroqNode", "Tachyum"]
by_label: dict[str, dict] = {}
for d in rows:
    if d["label"] not in by_label or d["perf"] > by_label[d["label"]]["perf"]:
        by_label[d["label"]] = d
items = [(by_label[n]["power"], by_label[n]["perf"], n) for n in curated if n in by_label]
place_labels(ax, fig, items, fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["ink"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.095, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11)

# Extent of the plotted rows, with and without the single lowest-power entry.
_la_lo = min(rows, key=lambda d: d["power"])
assert _la_lo["label"] == "Netcast" and sum(d["power"] == _la_lo["power"] for d in rows) == 1
_la_hi = max(d["power"] for d in rows)
_la_next = min(d["power"] for d in rows if d is not _la_lo)
la_floor_mw = f"{_la_lo['power'] * 1e3:.0f}"
la_next_mw = f"{_la_next * 1e3:.0f}"
la_orders_all = f"{np.log10(_la_hi / _la_lo['power']):.1f}"
la_orders_rest = f"{np.log10(_la_hi / _la_next):.1f}"
la_b200_pflops = f"{by_label['B200']['perf'] / 1e6:.1f}"
```

The points form a dense, heterogeneous cloud rather than clustering around a single operating point. That spread reflects deployment targets rather than a single ranking of designs, because the plotted points mix numerical precisions, supported operations, sparse and dense ratings, and chip, card, and system boundaries. The low end of the range also rests on one entry. The survey lists MIT's Netcast at `{python} la_floor_mw`\ mW with the note "Not truly embedded", and we could not establish what that power rating covers [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS]. Every other entry sits at `{python} la_next_mw`\ mW or above, so the span is `{python} la_orders_all` orders of magnitude with Netcast and `{python} la_orders_rest` without it. A subwatt sensor processor emphasizes local storage and low-precision arithmetic to avoid costly off-chip transfers, whereas a data-center accelerator devotes orders of magnitude more power to compute arrays and high-bandwidth memory. The survey places B200 at its `{python} la_b200_pflops`\ PFLOPS sparse rating, whereas the comparison below uses dense rates at the data-center end of that plane to show what happens when arithmetic grows faster than the memory that feeds it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Ratios for the GPU comparison, from the file that draws the figure.
import csv as _csv_bp
import _python.plots as _ap_bp
from pathlib import Path as _Path_bp

_bp_file = _Path_bp(_ap_bp.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "book/contents/chapters/02-pressures/data/fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier/chapter2-gpu-balance-point.csv"
with open(_bp_file, encoding="utf-8") as _fh:
    _bp = {r["Chip_Name"]: r for r in _csv_bp.DictReader(l for l in _fh if not l.startswith("#"))}


_bp_t, _bp_n = "Peak_FP16_Tensor_TFLOPS", "Peak_FP16_nonTensor_TFLOPS"


def _bp_bw(name):
    return float(_bp[name]["Memory_Bandwidth_GBs"])


def _bp_bal(name, col=_bp_t):
    # Each balance point stays on its own row of NVIDIA's tables.
    return float(_bp[name][col]) * 1000 / _bp_bw(name)


def _bp_x(col, start, end):
    return float(_bp[end][col]) / float(_bp[start][col])


_bp_half = "B200 HGX half sparse"
_bp_gb200 = "B200 GB200 NVL72 per GPU"
assert _bp["P100"][_bp_t] == "NA" and _bp["B200"][_bp_n] == "NA"
bp_nt_x = f"{_bp_x(_bp_n, 'P100', 'H100'):.1f}"
bp_hbm_nt = f"{_bp_bw('H100') / _bp_bw('P100'):.1f}"
bp_t_x = f"{_bp_x(_bp_t, 'V100', 'H100'):.1f}"
bp_hbm_t = f"{_bp_bw('H100') / _bp_bw('V100'):.1f}"
bp_t_x_b200 = f"{_bp_x(_bp_t, 'V100', 'B200'):.1f}"
bp_hbm_b200 = f"{_bp_bw('B200') / _bp_bw('V100'):.1f}"
bp_tdp = f"{float(_bp['B200']['TDP_Watts']) / float(_bp['P100']['TDP_Watts']):.1f}"
bp_nt_p100 = f"{_bp_bal('P100', _bp_n):.0f}"
bp_nt_a100 = f"{_bp_bal('A100', _bp_n):.0f}"
bp_nt_h100 = f"{_bp_bal('H100', _bp_n):.0f}"
bp_t_v100 = f"{_bp_bal('V100'):.0f}"
bp_t_h100 = f"{_bp_bal('H100'):.0f}"
bp_t_fold = f"{_bp_bal('H100') / _bp_bal('V100'):.1f}"
bp_hgx = f"{_bp_bal('B200'):.0f}"
bp_hgx_half = f"{_bp_bal(_bp_half):.0f}"
bp_gb200 = f"{_bp_bal(_bp_gb200):.0f}"
bp_gb200_pct = f"{100 * (_bp_bal(_bp_gb200) / _bp_bal('H100') - 1):.0f}"
bp_print_pct = f"{100 * (1 - _bp_bal('B200') / _bp_bal('H100')):.0f}"
bp_prior_pct = f"{100 * (_bp_bal('H100') / _bp_bal('A100') - 1):.0f}"
bp_step_rate = f"{_bp_x(_bp_t, 'H100', 'B200'):.1f}"
bp_step_bw = f"{_bp_bw('B200') / _bp_bw('H100'):.1f}"
bp_gb200_pf = f"{float(_bp[_bp_gb200][_bp_t]) / 1000:.1f}"
# The caption and alt text type these values; stop the build if they go stale.
assert (bp_nt_p100, bp_nt_h100, bp_t_v100, bp_t_h100, bp_hgx, bp_hgx_half, bp_gb200) == ("29", "40", "139", "295", "286", "292", "312")
assert (bp_t_x_b200, bp_hbm_b200, bp_tdp) == ("17.6", "8.6", "3.3")
```

Across five NVIDIA GPU generations from Pascal P100 (2016) to Blackwell B200 (2024) in its HGX configuration, NVIDIA rates half-precision floating-point (FP16) throughput on two separate rows, and a growth factor cannot be read across them. Non-Tensor FP16 on conventional floating-point cores grew `{python} bp_nt_x`$\times$ from P100 to H100 ($21.2\text{ to }133.8\ \text{TFLOPS}$), while off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) bandwidth grew `{python} bp_hbm_nt`$\times$ ($732\text{ to }3{,}352\ \text{GB/s}$) [@NVIDIA2016P100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @NVIDIA2020A100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper]. Dense FP16 on matrix Tensor Cores, which first appear in V100, grew `{python} bp_t_x`$\times$ from V100 to H100 ($125\text{ to }989.4\ \text{TFLOPS}$) against `{python} bp_hbm_t`$\times$ for HBM, and `{python} bp_t_x_b200`$\times$ from V100 to HGX B200 ($125\text{ to }2{,}200\ \text{TFLOPS}$) against `{python} bp_hbm_b200`$\times$ for HBM [@NVIDIA2017V100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief]. TDP rose `{python} bp_tdp`$\times$ from P100 to B200 ($300\text{ to }1{,}000\ \text{W}$) (@fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier a). NVIDIA's Blackwell tables print no non-Tensor FP16 rate, so that row stops at H100. Both comparisons hold precision fixed and exclude structured sparsity,[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02] and they span successive process nodes and, at B200, dual-reticle packaging.

[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02]: **Structured sparsity**: Sparse matrices contain zero values whose arithmetic can sometimes be skipped. Hardware-supported structured sparsity limits the patterns of nonzero values so that dedicated hardware can process the remaining values efficiently. Advertised sparse throughput assumes those patterns; the comparison here uses dense throughput throughout. The B200 value is the 2.2\ PFLOPS dense rate that NVIDIA's table prints; half of its 4.5\ PFLOPS sparse rating would be 2.25\ PFLOPS.

Because arithmetic capacity expanded faster than off-chip memory bandwidth, feeding these datapaths demands more data reuse inside the package. If we define a workload's *operational intensity* as the arithmetic operations executed per byte transferred across the HBM boundary, dividing peak compute rate by memory bandwidth gives the off-chip balance point plotted in @fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier b [@Williams2009Roofline]. The balance point must be read within one row. The non-Tensor FP16 balance point goes from `{python} bp_nt_p100`\ FLOP/byte on P100 to `{python} bp_nt_a100`\ FLOP/byte on A100 and back to `{python} bp_nt_h100`\ FLOP/byte on H100. The dense Tensor Core FP16 balance point rises `{python} bp_t_fold`-fold, from `{python} bp_t_v100`\ FLOP/byte on V100 to `{python} bp_t_h100`\ FLOP/byte on H100. Both H100 values rest on a $3{,}352\ \text{GB/s}$ whitepaper row marked not finalized [@NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper]. HGX B200 then gives `{python} bp_hgx`\ FLOP/byte, because its $7.7\ \text{TB/s}$ HBM3e bandwidth grows `{python} bp_step_bw`$\times$ alongside the `{python} bp_step_rate`$\times$ step in dense Tensor Core FP16. We plot HGX B200 because NVIDIA's table for it prints the dense rate, bandwidth, and TDP together, but that apparent plateau does not survive a change of configuration or rounding. Half of the table's sparse rating gives `{python} bp_hgx_half`\ FLOP/byte, and the rack-scale GB200 NVL72 works out to `{python} bp_gb200_pf`\ PFLOPS and $8\ \text{TB/s}$ per GPU, which gives `{python} bp_gb200`\ FLOP/byte, `{python} bp_gb200_pct`% above H100 [@NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief]. The specifications therefore show that the Tensor Core balance point's climb slowed, from `{python} bp_prior_pct`% between A100 and H100 to a range of `{python} bp_print_pct`% below to `{python} bp_gb200_pct`% above H100 at B200. They do not show that it stopped. A dense FP16 kernel operating below that balance point cannot saturate the matrix engines even with zero control stalls. Greater on-chip data reuse raises the kernel's operational intensity by reducing HBM traffic, whereas more HBM bandwidth lowers the hardware's balance point at a fixed peak compute rate.

![**Arithmetic scaling outpaced off-chip memory bandwidth through H100.** (a) Non-Tensor FP16, dense Tensor Core FP16, HBM bandwidth, and TDP for five GPU generations (2016–2024), each relative to its own V100 value; no growth factor crosses the FP16 rows. (b) Within a row, the off-chip balance point is 29, 50, and 40\ FLOP/byte for non-Tensor FP16 on P100, A100, and H100, and rises from 139 to 295 for dense Tensor Core FP16 (V100 to H100); the plotted HGX B200 gives 286, and other B200 ratings give 292 to 312. Hardware specifications exclude structured sparsity [@NVIDIA2016P100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @NVIDIA2017V100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2020A100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief].](images/fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier){#fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel chart for P100, V100, A100, H100, and B200 GPUs from 2016 to 2024. First panel plots each series against its own V100 value: dense Tensor Core FP16 reaches 17.6 times on B200 while HBM bandwidth reaches 8.6 times and TDP 3.3 times, and non-Tensor FP16 stops at H100. Second panel shows the off-chip balance point as separate bars for each row: non-Tensor FP16 goes from 29 floating-point operations per byte transferred from HBM on P100 to 50 on A100 and 40 on H100, and dense Tensor Core FP16 rises from 139 on V100 to 295 on H100 and 286 on HGX B200."}

### Why Accelerators Coupled the Hardware and Software Stacks

This divergence between arithmetic density and memory supply erodes the classical separation of concerns inside an accelerator design, because the reuse that keeps the arrays fed depends on the dataflow, the on-chip memory, and the compiler schedule at once. Whereas a conventional processor stack lets compiler writers, microarchitects, and process engineers work against relatively independent interfaces, @fig-tao-vs-taos contrasts that modular hierarchy with the coupled regime of domain-specific hardware, in which a single power, thermal, and area envelope ties all three layers together.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override Top-only placement left 233 pt blank at the bottom of the page before the next heading in the CI Springer render (float-induced-whitespace, run 42260053514). -->
![**Specialization makes cross-layer dependencies explicit.** (a) A classical layered view separates optimization, architecture, and technology into modular tiers. (b) The specialization-coupled view reveals how domain specialization binds software mapping, microarchitecture, and silicon fabrication across shared power, thermal, and area constraints.](images/fig-tao-vs-taos){#fig-tao-vs-taos width="80%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Two side-by-side stack diagrams. The first panel shows optimization, architecture, and technology stacked in a top-down hierarchy. The second panel introduces a specialization block coupled across all three tiers, bounded by a shared thermal, power, and area constraint perimeter."}

Specialization does not invent cross-layer coupling, but it removes the slack that once hid it. An architect who chooses a systolic or tensor-core array geometry fixes which dataflows keep operands local. Sizing the on-chip scratchpad to sustain that reuse then sets die area and wire reach, and those layout choices determine clock frequency and leakage in the chosen process node. An architectural model that evaluates datapath throughput without accounting for on-chip storage area and physical wire delay can misrank candidates inside the block. Even when a block's internal datapath, storage, and wires are well balanced, however, its value still depends on how it fits into the surrounding system.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

## Balancing Specialization and System Composition

A specialized engine delivers a system speedup only when the surrounding machine can supply its inputs and use its outputs. The host still executes control flow, the runtime moves data and synchronizes execution, and shared memories and links serve other clients. The architect must therefore compare complete organizations, including the software and communication needed to use each block, before deciding which specialized capability is worth its area and power.

### From Kernel Efficiency to System Speedup

Specialization can produce large local gains by removing general-purpose machinery. For the H.264 video encoder studied by @HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency, a fixed-function application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), with numbers scaled from 180\ nm to 90\ nm, improved energy efficiency roughly `{python} he_stated_asic`-fold relative to a four-core chip multiprocessor, by the factor the source states in its text. The base-chip energies behind such factors are simulator estimates, which the authors give as within 30% of actual energy, so the result fixes the scale of the gain and not its exact value. The source's tables give about `{python} he_tables_asic`-fold, from the base chip's `{python} he_base_mj`\ mJ per frame over the ASIC's `{python} he_asic_mj`\ mJ, and a 30% band on the base energy alone spans about `{python} he_band_lo` to `{python} he_band_hi`, which covers both values.[^fn-hameed-factors-c02] We use the stated `{python} he_stated_asic` because only the text supplies one consistent set of factors for the steps between the base chip and the ASIC, and either value makes the same point. @fig-ch02-specialization-energy traces that gain through each step toward the ASIC and shows where the base processors spent their energy.

[^fn-hameed-factors-c02]: **The stated factors**: The source does not reconcile its text and tables, and rounding in the ASIC's one-digit value cannot close the gap, since even `{python} he_asic_mj_hi`\ mJ would give `{python} he_tables_asic_lo`. Our read of the bar heights in the source's per-stage energy chart gives about `{python} he_read_simd` for the first step, where the text states `{python} he_stated_simd`, and about `{python} he_read_asic` for the ASIC.


![**Reaching the ASIC took removing overhead and customizing the arithmetic.** (a) Energy efficiency of a 720p H.264 encoder as a four-processor 90\ nm chip gains single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) and very-long-instruction-word instructions, fused operations, and custom instructions, compared with an ASIC scaled from 180\ nm, using the factors stated in the source's text. (b) Base-processor energy by component across the encoder, as tabulated in the source [@HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency].](images/fig-ch02-specialization-energy){#fig-ch02-specialization-energy width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel horizontal bar chart. Panel (a) shows energy efficiency on a log scale relative to base processors: 7 times with those instructions, 10 times with operation fusion, 170 times with custom instructions, and 500 times for the ASIC. Panel (b) shows base-processor energy shares: instruction fetch 33.6 percent, pipeline registers 22.0 percent, data cache 19.2 percent, control 9.7 percent, register file 9.7 percent, and functional units 5.8 percent."}

In these estimates, functional units account for only `{python} he_fu_pct`% of the base processors' energy, while instruction fetch alone takes `{python} he_if_pct`%. Wider datapaths and fused operations recover only about one order of magnitude. Treating every component except the functional units as overhead would yield only about `{python} he_non_fu_ratio`$\times$ from these totals, and 20$\times$ in the source's own statement. We read both as low estimates, an inference the source does not state, because the base machine counts the energy of full 32-bit functional units and so overstates what those units need. The source still judges that margin far short of the ASIC, and it concludes that approaching ASIC efficiency takes both customized functional units and the removal of almost all other overhead. Customization starts before the custom-instruction step, since the SIMD units already use custom-width functional units in place of standard 32-bit versions. The size of the ASIC's gain explains the attraction of specialization, but the fraction of the application accelerated and the cost of reaching the block determine how much benefit survives in a full system.

Amdahl's law makes this distinction explicit. If a fraction $f$ of baseline execution receives a local speedup $S_{\mathrm{accel}}$, the total speedup including communication is

$$S_{\mathrm{total}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \frac{f}{S_{\mathrm{accel}}} + t_{\mathrm{comm}}}$${#eq-amdahl-communication}

where $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ is the added, nonoverlapped transfer and synchronization time normalized to baseline execution time. Even with free communication, an infinitely fast accelerator cannot exceed $1/(1-f)$ total speedup because the unaccelerated host work in @eq-amdahl-communication remains [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]; communication lowers that ceiling further.

How strongly this bound limits a design depends on the workload. Under Gustafson's law, a system can increase its parallel work as more processors become available, as a training study might do with a larger model or dataset [@Gustafson1988AmdahlLaw]. A latency-critical mobile extended-reality (XR) pipeline instead has fixed per-frame work and a deadline. Dispatch and synchronization consume time that extra arithmetic units cannot recover.

The LogCA accelerator model separates the costs hidden inside the communication term [@AltafWood2017LogCA]. The useful distinction here is between a fixed cost paid for each invocation and a data-transfer cost that grows with the work. For a simple offload with no overlap, completion time is the sum of invocation time, accelerator execution time, and transfer time. Offloading helps only when that sum is smaller than execution on an optimized host.

Consider a neural processing unit (NPU) invoked separately for each small layer of a neural network. Command preparation, queue submission, and synchronization can consume much of the elapsed time even when the matrix arithmetic finishes quickly. Fusing layers or batching requests places more useful work behind each launch and can move the workload beyond its break-even payload size. But batching alone cannot remove a transfer cost that grows in proportion to the arithmetic. If moving each additional operation's data takes at least as much time as offloading saves on that operation, no larger payload makes the nonoverlapped offload profitable. The design needs fewer transferred bytes, more link bandwidth, or effective overlap.

These remedies cross different boundaries. A compiler may retain intermediate tensors on chip and reduce traffic without changing the interface. A lower-cost submission path changes how the runtime invokes the accelerator, while a wider physical link changes the hardware. The actual launch path, achieved bandwidth, data reuse, and host baseline determine which remedy helps; a link specification alone cannot settle the comparison. An empirical sweep across payload sizes tests where, if anywhere, the complete offload becomes faster than host execution.

Our sweep on one Apple-silicon laptop times 32-bit floating-point matrix products on the CPU, through its vendor library, and on the integrated GPU, through PyTorch (@fig-ch02-offload-break-even). Across `{python} ob_runs` consecutive runs in one session, a single $n \times n$ product first beat the host at $n$ between `{python} ob_res` with its operands already on the GPU and between `{python} ob_copy` with copies in and out. ![**Launch cost sets a floor, and batching moves the break-even toward smaller matrices.** Median time for 32-bit floating-point matrix products on an Apple M5 Max on battery power, in `{python} ob_runs` consecutive runs drawn as separate lines: (a) one product on the host CPU and on the GPU, with operands resident or copied in and out; (b) sixteen products on the host and on the GPU, waiting for each launch or issued as one. CPU and GPU share memory here, so the copies do not cross a discrete link. Crossovers describe this one session and machine.](images/fig-ch02-offload-break-even){#fig-ch02-offload-break-even width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel log-log line chart of median time against matrix dimension from 16 to 3072, with five lines per series for five runs. The GPU's flat floor at small sizes is the fixed invocation cost that LogCA isolates, and only enough work behind each launch can repay it. At small sizes, which we take as $n \le 256$, waiting on sixteen launches costs about `{python} ob_launch_ratio` times as much as one launch in the pooled medians, and between `{python} ob_launch_lo` and `{python} ob_launch_hi` times at individual sizes within a run. The sweep supports the direction of two remedies, batching and avoiding copies, without supplying a design constant, and it did not test fusion or a cheaper submission path. Its host also kept only about one of the machine's eighteen cores busy, so a host using more cores would likely push these crossovers to larger $n$.[^fn-offload-spread-c02] Copy time grows with $n$ here, but a dense product moves on the order of $n^2$ values for $n^3$ operations, so the arithmetic outgrows the transfers as the matrix grows, and a discrete link would not change that scaling. The case in which no payload size reaches break-even therefore remains untested, and testing it takes a kernel whose transfers grow as fast as its arithmetic.

[^fn-offload-spread-c02]: **Spread across runs**: The one-launch crossover held across these runs, whereas the others moved by a full step of the size grid, a shift that one run cannot reveal. That step measures spread within this session, not the full range of the resident and copy crossovers. The lower end of the copy range also depends on the statistic, because `{python} ob_copy_low_runs` of the `{python} ob_runs` runs crosses at `{python} ob_copy_low` by median time, whereas comparing mean times puts all of them at `{python} ob_copy_mean`. Three earlier runs on the same machine, on AC power with an older PyTorch release and set aside because their sixteen-launch arm waited only once, crossed at `{python} ob_old_res` with resident operands. With copies, one of them led the host at `{python} ob_gap_lead`, fell behind at `{python} ob_gap_back`, and led again from `{python} ob_gap_again`. The one-launch crossover stayed at `{python} ob_one` in those runs as well.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The unamortized offload wall"}
**The trap.** A team treats the local matrix-multiply acceleration of an NPU as the expected system speedup.

**The mechanism.** Small layers may contain too little work to amortize each invocation, while input and output transfers add costs that grow with the workload. An optimized host can also erase an apparent gain measured against scalar code.

**The lesson.** Compare complete offloads against optimized host execution. Test whether fusion, batching, local reuse, or a cheaper submission path changes the result. If feasible changes still leave the offload below break-even, retaining host execution is the supported choice.
:::

The offload comparison thus requires more than a faster datapath. It needs a workable mapping and invocation path, and it may require changing the boundary between software and hardware. Integrating the resulting blocks adds a further set of physical and behavioral constraints.

### Packaging and Wafer-Scale Communication {#sec-wafer-scale-communication-tradeoffs}

Partitioning a large design into chiplets can improve manufacturing yield under random-defect models, let different functions use separate process nodes, and spread development cost across products. Those benefits must pay for packaging, test, assembly losses, and die-to-die communication [@Murphy1964CostSize; @FengMa2022ChipletActuary]. A partition that looks favorable in a block diagram may require more bandwidth than the available die edge can carry. The bandwidth available per unit of edge, or *shoreline bandwidth density*, depends on interface placement, connection pitch, and signaling rate, so the partition and the package have to be evaluated together.

Standard interfaces reduce part of the integration burden. Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) specifies die-to-die physical layers and protocols [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec], and a test standard lets defective chiplets be screened before assembly [@IEEE2020Std1838]. Neither establishes that the finished system has enough power, cooling, or bandwidth, and screened chiplets can still carry undetected defects or fail in assembly.

Keeping compute and storage on a wafer changes these trade-offs rather than removing them. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine keeps communication on a large compute and SRAM fabric [@Cerebras2019WSE], reducing reliance on board-level links while requiring specialized power delivery, cooling, and defect tolerance. In a wafer-scale GPU design study, a 300\ mm wafer could house about 100 GPU modules, yet physical constraints allowed only about 40 [@PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU]. Available silicon area therefore does not directly determine usable compute; placement, defect routing, and software scheduling determine which resources a workload can exploit.

Beyond those physical limits on bandwidth, power, and usable area, block composition creates failures that do not appear when modules are checked separately. Third-party intellectual property (IP) delivered as hard macros, already laid out and fixed, or as encrypted RTL restricts integration teams to documented behavior, supplied models, and accessible interfaces [@Arm2013CortexA15HardMacro; @Intel2024EncryptedRTLIP]. Even when blocks implement a standard bus [@Arm2020AXI], incompatible assumptions about reset order, power-up sequence, or clock domains can prevent them from operating together. A search cannot safely treat missing compatibility information as permission to combine blocks, and obtaining that information consumes engineering time before performance evaluation can begin.

### Choosing the System Boundary

The same composition problem extends beyond a package. A candidate accelerator may finish its own kernel sooner yet send enough extra traffic across a shared fabric to delay the end-to-end request. Whenever an interaction can reverse which design wins, the evaluation boundary must include it. The progression from cores to warehouse-scale systems in @fig-architecture-levers identifies the additional obligations that arise as that boundary expands.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The tall print-size scale diagram needs a full-page float option near its discussion. -->
![**The study boundary must include interactions that can change the decision.** Stacked from warehouse-scale deployment at the top down to core execution at the bottom, five compute scales illustrate how comparison obligations funnel outward as the system boundary expands upward from a core. A broader study may reuse component models; it need not reproduce every lower-level detail at the same fidelity.](images/fig-architecture-levers){#fig-architecture-levers width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram of five architecture scales stacked from warehouse-scale system at the top down through wafer-scale system, system-on-chip or chiplet, accelerator, and core at the bottom, funneling outward as the system boundary expands upward from core to warehouse-scale. Each scale adds named obligations to a common comparison path feeding one cross-scale architecture comparison."}

At warehouse scale, placement and sharing decisions couple servers, networks, distributed runtimes, cooling, and facility power [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Within and across nodes, cache-coherent interconnects such as Compute Express Link (CXL) make pooled memory another architectural choice [@CXLConsortium2026CXL]. These mechanisms belong inside the study when they can change its target metric, whether tail latency, sustained throughput, or total cost.

A broader boundary does not require cycle-level simulation of every component, because architects can combine characterized component models with trace-driven or discrete-event simulation, hardware testbeds, and production telemetry as long as the combination preserves the interactions that matter. Independent trace replays can miss shared-network contention, for example, while mean response times hide stragglers that govern tail latency at scale [@DeanBarroso2013TailAtScale]. An architect therefore seeks the smallest boundary that still captures interactions capable of flipping which design wins, keeping evaluation cost manageable without assuming those effects away.

Within that boundary, a hardware organization still needs software that can use it. The offload example shows why compiler mappings and runtime behavior belong in the comparison, and why changing either can alter the value of hardware that is already fixed.

## Workload Volatility and Software–Hardware Coupling

A compiler can fuse operations into a payload large enough to amortize an accelerator launch, or introduce spills that erase the expected saving. The evaluation therefore needs an executable path to compile, schedule, and drive the candidate hardware. That path continues to change after silicon is fixed, creating two related pressures: making a specialized mechanism usable and keeping it useful as workloads evolve.

### Why Hardware Gains Require a Working Compiler Path

A custom matrix unit or instruction extension can excel in a hand-coded microbenchmark yet remain idle in an application if no compiler pass, kernel library, or runtime can use it effectively. An *executable software path* connects the programming model through compilation and libraries to the runtime, driver or firmware, and deployment controls. Different systems require different components, but the path must be complete enough to run the intended workload without losing the hardware benefit to extra transfers, spills, or dispatch overhead.

To avoid repeating most of that work for every target, a *compiler narrow waist* shares a common intermediate representation (IR) on which general transformations operate before target-specific lowering maps operations onto a particular machine. Halide separates an algorithm from its execution schedule [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM], while Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) supports transformations across levels of abstraction [@LattnerEtAl2020MLIR].[^fn-mlir-dialects-c02] Although these abstractions reduce duplication, every target still needs lowering, runtime support, and validation suited to its hardware.

[^fn-mlir-dialects-c02]: **MLIR dialects**: MLIR groups operations into modular dialects, each at one level of abstraction, from tensor algebra (`linalg`) through loops and arithmetic down to LLVM IR or hardware-specific dialects. A computation is lowered step by step through these dialects, so each optimization can run where the information it needs, such as tensor shapes or loop bounds, is still explicit.

The path in @fig-codegen-narrow-waist locates that shared representation between source programs and target execution. A matrix instruction needs a lowering path that matches its operand layout; an asynchronous transfer engine needs scheduling and synchronization that preserve correctness. Those obligations connect compiler work directly to whether an architectural candidate can be evaluated at all.

![**Executable target software paths connect developer intent to verification checks.** High-level domain-specific abstract syntax trees (Python, Triton domain-specific languages) lower through mid-level control-data flow graphs in MLIR dialects and LLVM IR at the compiler narrow waist, where workload intent, architectural mechanisms such as CPU instruction-set extensions and NPU dataflows, and silicon constraints converge. Lowered machine code and runtimes then pass through verification checks for correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability.](images/fig-codegen-narrow-waist){#fig-codegen-narrow-waist width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of an executable target software path showing programming models, compiler representations, libraries, runtimes, and generated code connecting hardware constraints to correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability checks."}

They wrap instructions for SM90, an architecture CUTLASS already carried at v3.0.0, so the step records wider coverage of existing hardware rather than a new target, and the counts do not show whether people wrote these files or a tool generated them. Architecture-specific lines then grew only `{python} sw_cut_plateau`% from v4.0.0 to v4.7.0, and the inline assembly count was `{python} sw_cut_asm` at both tags. Although such counts cannot price the work, shared compilers reduce duplication across targets and hand-tuned libraries expose hardware features before general compilers support them, and both routes must still produce a working binary that the evaluation can run.

Once code reaches the target, its mapping can determine whether the offload pays. Fusing operations places more work behind each invocation while retaining intermediate tensors on chip reduces traffic, addressing the two distinct costs identified by LogCA. Yet fusion also keeps more values live at once, increasing register pressure so that when live values exceed the available registers, the compiler spills them to memory and can undo the locality gain.

The RISC-V Vector extension makes the trade-off concrete. A compiler can group architectural vector registers to process more elements per instruction, but wider groups leave fewer independent groups for other live values [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. A fused kernel may therefore benefit from wide grouping until register spills add enough traffic to slow it down. Peak vector width cannot determine the winner; compiled execution with the intended data types and workload can.

Whereas an autotuner such as AutoTVM searches compiler schedules on a fixed machine [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM], a joint hardware–software study varies the machine as well, so each hardware–schedule pair needs a fair evaluation. A study that holds one candidate's schedule fixed while tuning another can mistake software effort for architectural merit, which makes building and checking executable compiler paths part of the cost of comparing hardware alternatives rather than a step that follows the architecture decision.

### Changing Software and Fixed Hardware {#sec-software-changes-faster-than-silicon}

An architectural comparison may become outdated while a chip is still being specified, verified, and fabricated. A memory hierarchy tuned for one model family and compiler release can encounter different tensor shapes, kernel schedules, and serving regimes at deployment. Before tapeout, hardware and software teams can revise the design together, although late hardware changes become expensive. After tapeout, software has to adapt the fixed machine.

Numerical formats make this commitment especially clear. Supporting 8-bit floating-point (FP8), 4-bit integer, or block-scale representations changes the arithmetic units and datapaths built into silicon. Block-scale formats share exponent or scale metadata across groups of elements [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling], so their efficiency depends on a specific organization of values and metadata. A model that adopts a different format after the datapath is frozen may no longer use the hardware as efficiently. The architect must decide which workload properties are stable enough to specialize and where programmability is worth its area and energy cost.

Memory behavior can change just as sharply. Convolutional inference with fixed frame sizes follows a relatively regular schedule, whereas autoregressive Transformer serving retains a growing key-value (KV) cache of attention keys and values from earlier tokens to avoid recomputing them [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention], so variable sequence lengths continually change the amount of stored state. Mixture-of-experts models further route inputs to selected expert subnetworks [@ShazeerEtAl2017MoE], making traffic depend on the input, while prompt processing and incremental token generation form distinct prefill and decode phases [@AgrawalEtAl2024SarathiServe]. Because these shifts alter how computation and memory traffic arrive, a larger working set can overflow a scratchpad and force transfers to dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), while a smaller serving batch can leave too little work to amortize each accelerator invocation. The relevant question is which assumption changed and whether the hardware retains enough flexibility to accommodate it.

Compute demand is moving just as quickly. Epoch AI reported a four- to fivefold annual increase in training compute for notable models through May 2024 [@SevillaRoldan2024ComputeGrowth]. A frozen July 2026 snapshot of the same database shows the trend (@fig-training-compute-growth) [@EpochAI2025AIModels].

```{python}
#| label: fig-training-compute-growth
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Reported and estimated training compute rises about 4.4-fold per year in this historical sample.**
#|   The 467 displayed records come from a frozen July 2026 snapshot of the Epoch AI database [@EpochAI2025AIModels].
#|   Compute is plotted logarithmically against publication date (2010–2026); it combines reported figures with
#|   source estimates of differing confidence, including speculative estimates. Filled points use the snapshot's
#|   frontier flag (top five by training compute at release). The line is an
#|   unweighted least-squares fit to the logarithm of compute. Its $\approx 4.4\times$ annual growth factor
#|   characterizes this sample and does not measure how changes in model scale intersect hardware development schedules.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale scatter plot of 467 reported or source-estimated AI training-compute values versus publication date from 2010 to 2026. Filled points mark the snapshot's frontier models. An unweighted fitted line marks roughly 4.4-fold growth per year. AlexNet, AlphaGo Zero, GPT-3, and GPT-4 are labeled; all records used in the fit are visible."

import csv
import datetime
import math
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _year(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "book/contents/chapters/02-pressures/data/fig-training-compute-growth/chapter2-training-compute.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for row in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        yr = _year(row["publication_date"])
        try:
            flop = float(row["training_compute_flop"])
        except ValueError:
            flop = None
        if yr and flop and flop > 0 and 2010 <= yr <= 2026.6:
            pts.append({"yr": yr, "flop": flop, "name": row["model"], "frontier": row["frontier"] == "1"})

years = np.array([p["yr"] for p in pts])
logf = np.array([math.log10(p["flop"]) for p in pts])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(years, logf, 1)
growth = 10 ** slope

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.3))
other = [p for p in pts if not p["frontier"]]
front = [p for p in pts if p["frontier"]]
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in other], [p["flop"] for p in other], s=8, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=2, label="Notable models")
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in front], [p["flop"] for p in front], s=12, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["workload"], edgecolor=COLORS["workload_ink"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=3, label="Frontier models")
xline = np.array([2010, 2026.5])
ax.plot(xline, 10 ** (intercept + slope * xline), color=COLORS["constraints"], lw=1.5, zorder=4)
ax.text(2018.0, 10 ** (intercept + slope * 2018.8), f"×{growth:.1f} per year", fontsize=6.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], rotation=29, rotation_mode="anchor",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9))

by_name = {p["name"]: p for p in pts}
landmarks = {"AlexNet": ("AlexNet", 6, -12), "AlphaGo Zero": ("AlphaGo Zero", -8, 11),
             "GPT-3 175B (davinci)": ("GPT-3", -8, 11), "GPT-4 (Jun 2023)": ("GPT-4", 6, 10)}
for key, (label, dx, dy) in landmarks.items():
    p = by_name.get(key)
    if p:
        ax.annotate(label, (p["yr"], p["flop"]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(dx, dy),
                    fontsize=5.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"],
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["muted"], lw=0.45))

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(2010, 2026.7)
ax.set_ylim(5e13, 3e27)
ax.set_xlabel("Publication date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Reported or estimated training compute (FLOP)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2010, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2022, 2025])
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_spine].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.14, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Sensitivity of the fit above to its date window: same rows, same regression.
_tc = []
with open(_root / "book/contents/chapters/02-pressures/data/fig-training-compute-growth/chapter2-training-compute.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for row in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        _tc.append((_year(row["publication_date"]), float(row["training_compute_flop"])))


def _tc_growth(first, last):
    kept = [(y, f) for y, f in _tc if first <= y <= last]
    return 10 ** np.polyfit([y for y, _ in kept], [math.log10(f) for _, f in kept], 1)[0]


# The caption's 467 and 4.4 are typed; these stop the build if they go stale.
assert len(pts) == 467 and f"{growth:.1f}" == "4.4"
tc_all = len(_tc)
tc_dropped = sum(y < 2010 for y, _ in _tc)
assert tc_all - tc_dropped == len(pts)
tc_oldest = int(min(y for y, _ in _tc))
tc_from_2000 = f"{_tc_growth(2000, 2030):.1f}"
tc_from_2005 = f"{_tc_growth(2005, 2030):.1f}"
tc_from_2015 = f"{_tc_growth(2015, 2030):.1f}"
tc_to_2024 = f"{_tc_growth(2010, 2024):.1f}"
tc_through_2024 = f"{_tc_growth(2010, 2024.9999):.1f}"
tc_every_record = f"{_tc_growth(0, 3000):.1f}"
tc_from_2018 = f"{_tc_growth(2018, 2030):.1f}"
_tc_cov = np.polyfit(years, logf, 1, cov=True)[1]
_tc_se = math.sqrt(_tc_cov[0, 0])
# Normal approximation; the residual degrees of freedom are 465.
tc_ci_lo = f"{10 ** (slope - 1.96 * _tc_se):.1f}"
tc_ci_hi = f"{10 ** (slope + 1.96 * _tc_se):.1f}"
```

The fitted rate depends on the window. The line starts at 2010 and so leaves out the `{python} tc_dropped` of `{python} tc_all` records dated earlier, the oldest from `{python} tc_oldest`. The same regression gives `{python} tc_from_2000`-fold per year from 2000, `{python} tc_from_2005`-fold from 2005, `{python} tc_from_2015`-fold from 2015, and `{python} tc_from_2018`-fold from 2018. A window that closes at the start of 2024 gives `{python} tc_to_2024`-fold, one that closes at the end of 2024 gives `{python} tc_through_2024`-fold, and a fit across every record gives `{python} tc_every_record`-fold. The fit's own 95% interval of `{python} tc_ci_lo` to `{python} tc_ci_hi`-fold is narrower than that spread and treats the records as independent draws, which a selected sample is not. This sample therefore supports rapid growth rather than one exact rate.

Larger training runs do not automatically change the underlying kernel mix, but performance measured at one model scale or serving regime does not transfer to another without re-evaluating memory traffic and software assumptions.

Deployment requirements can also change what a throughput number means without changing the arithmetic or the reported hardware. The matched MLPerf submissions below illustrate one such pressure by comparing standard and interactive latency requirements on the same named systems.

```{python}
ml12_int_ttft = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['interactive_ttft_ms']):,}"
```
